claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is primarily governed by kinetic suppression of atomic diffusion rather than thermodynamic entropy stabilization alone.
Atomic size mismatch produces pronounced lattice distortions in the proposed nanoalloy.
Local chemical ordering contributes to suppression of atomic diffusion.
Designing a composition to maximize atomic size mismatch will produce significant lattice distortion and local chemical ordering at room temperature.
Oxidation or extraneous reactions could confound measurements of diffusion and ordering during high-temperature exposure.
Lattice distortions and local chemical ordering create kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion.
Local lattice strain raises the energy barrier for atomic rearrangement.
Slower atomic rearrangement suppresses phase segregation and structural degradation.
The proposed kinetic barrier enhances both structural and chemical stability at high temperature.
A high-mismatch nanoalloy will have a lower atomic diffusion rate than a comparable lower-mismatch nanoalloy under identical thermal exposure.
A high-mismatch nanoalloy will show delayed or reduced phase segregation relative to the lower-mismatch baseline.
The high-mismatch nanoalloy will show smaller changes in lattice parameters and a more stable phase distribution over time.
The lower-mismatch baseline is expected to show higher diffusion rates and earlier phase separation.
The prediction applies only in a temperature window where atoms are mobile but thermal energy has not overcome the proposed distortion-induced kinetic barriers.
The prediction does not apply after significant coarsening, melting, or drastic phase transformation begins.
The prediction is limited to nanoscale dimensions for which surface effects do not dominate stability.
